analysis.one_liner: Caps bank overdraft fees at one per month, six per year, with clearer disclosure and consent rules.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing and no vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee from May 2016 until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Overdraft 'protection' is when a bank covers a purchase that exceeds your balance and charges a flat fee, often $30 or more per transaction, even for a small debit card purchase. This bill would cap those fees at one per month and six per year, require banks to show the fee as an interest rate so shoppers can compare it to other credit, stop charging fees when the only problem is a pending hold larger than the purchase, and ban fees for declining an ATM or debit card transaction. Banks that collect billions a year in overdraft and bounced-transaction fees would lose that revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who occasionally overdraw their accounts, especially low- and moderate-income households. The bill's own findings state that these fees have 'placed significant financial burdens on low- and moderate-income consumers' [S3]. A person who overdraws several times in one month would see fees drop from multiple $30-plus charges to at most one, and would get same-day notice when a fee hits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who overdraw their bank accounts

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, and requires fees to be 'reasonable and proportional' to the overdraft amount [S3].

Bans overdraft fees when the overdraft comes only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase, and bans non-sufficient-fund fees on ATM and debit card transactions — so customers can't be charged for a transaction that was never paid [S3].

Requires banks to disclose the overdraft fee as an annual percentage rate, disclose alternatives like linked accounts and lines of credit, show all overdraft fees on monthly statements, exclude available overdraft coverage from the displayed balance, and warn and let customers cancel an ATM or teller transaction that would trigger a fee [S3].

Requires written or electronic consent before a bank can charge overdraft fees on ATM or point-of-sale debit transactions, and stops banks from reporting negative information to credit bureaus when the overdraft and fees are repaid under the program [S3].
Imposes a one-year freeze on overdraft fee increases starting at enactment, and directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write the implementing rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions — banks and credit unions. Overdraft and non-sufficient-fund fees are a large, recurring revenue line for them; the bill caps the number and size of those fees, bans fees on declined ATM/debit transactions, and forces new disclosures and a fee freeze [S3]. Banks argue some of that revenue offsets the cost and risk of covering customers' shortfalls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: If fees are capped, banks may simply decline to cover overdrafts more often. A customer's rent check or utility payment could then bounce, triggering a fee from the merchant or landlord instead — the cost moves rather than disappears [S3].

Banks say overdraft coverage is a voluntary service that lets essential purchases go through; the bill's fee caps and consent rules reduce revenue that some institutions use to subsidize free checking accounts, which could push monthly maintenance fees up for all customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who actually pay these fees — typically customers living close to zero — the bill is a direct, sizable savings, and its disclosures address the marketing practices the findings call unfair and deceptive [S3]. The genuine cost is uncertain: some overdrafts that would have been paid will instead be declined, and the expense may shift to bounced-item fees charged by landlords and merchants rather than vanish. On balance the design targets the harshest practices — repeated same-day fees, holds-triggered fees, fees for declined transactions — rather than banning overdraft coverage outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee on May 11, 2016, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on May 11, 2016, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which holds jurisdiction over banking laws [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft and non-sufficient-fund fees kept charging them uncapped for the rest of the Congress; consumers who overdraw their accounts kept paying. The bill's sponsor gained nothing, and the problem it addressed continued through later Congresses with near-identical bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks collecting overdraft fees, not customers

for.name: Rep. Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as protecting consumers from abusive overdraft fee practices.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; sole jurisdiction over banking legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining eight months of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Democrats; the committee that took no action was chaired by a Republican, and no Republican cosponsor appears in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Overdraft and non-sufficient-fund fees are a major revenue line for depository institutions; the bill caps them at one per month and six per year, bans fees on declined ATM/debit transactions and on hold-inflated overdrafts, and freezes fee increases for a year [S3]. The industry's interest in this bill runs against the consumers who pay the fees, whom the bill's findings say are disproportionately low- and moderate-income [S3].
The bill bars banks from reporting negative information to credit bureaus when overdrafts and fees are repaid under a coverage program, removing a source of adverse data [S3].
